t: The Big Bang: How the Universe Began
d: 13.8 billion years ago the universe was hot, dense and expanding. Here is what happened in the first seconds, minutes and 380,000 years, and how we know.
x: The Big Bang is not an explosion in space. It is the expansion of space itself from an extremely hot, dense early state about 13.8 billion years ago . Every distant galaxy is moving away from every other, like raisins in rising dough. The first moments # A timeline of the first 380,000 years 0 – 10⁻⁴³ s : Planck era. Known physics breaks down; gravity and quantum mechanics would need to be unified. ~10⁻³⁶ – 10⁻³² s : Inflation. Space expands by a factor of at least 10²⁶ in a tiny fraction of a second, smoothing the universe and stretching quantum ripples into the seeds of galaxies. 10⁻¹² s : The electroweak force splits; particles gain mass through the Higgs field. 10⁻⁶ s : Quarks bind into protons and neutrons. A tiny excess of matter over antimatter (about 1 part in a billion) survives annihilation; everything we see comes from it. 1 s : Neutrinos decouple and stream freely (they still fill space as a cosmic neutrino background). 3 – 20 min : Big Bang nucleosynthesis. The universe acts as a fusion reactor, making ~75% hydrogen, ~25% helium and traces of lithium by mass. ~50,000 yr : Matter starts to dominate over radiation; dark matter begins clumping. 380,000 yr : Recombination. At ~3,000 K electrons join nuclei to make atoms, the universe becomes transparent, and the light released is the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Four pillars of evidence # Expansion. Edwin Hubble (building on Henrietta Leavitt’s Cepheid work and Vesto Slipher’s redshifts) showed in 1929 that galaxies recede faster the farther away they are. Georges Lemaître had proposed an expanding universe from a ‘primeval atom’ in 1927. The cosmic microwave background. Found by accident by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson in 1965, it is a near-perfect 2.725 K glow from every direction. Its tiny ripples (1 part in 100,000) were mapped by COBE, WMAP and Planck. Light elements. The measured cosmic abundances of hydrogen, helium and deuterium match the predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis. Evolution over time. Distant (younger) galaxies look different from nearby ones: smaller, bluer and messier, exactly what JWST sees at record distances. What the Big Bang does not explain # Open questions What came ‘before’, or whether ‘before’ makes sense. Time itself may begin with the Big Bang. What drove inflation. It is supported by the CMB’s flatness and fluctuation pattern but not directly proven (gravitational-wave ‘B-modes’ have not been found). Why there is more matter than antimatter. The Hubble tension. Local measurements give ~73 km/s/Mpc while the CMB predicts ~67.4; the CCHP team finds ~70.4. See Research: cosmology . Next: The Dark Ages and first stars .

t: The Cosmic Microwave Background: Baby Picture of the Universe
d: The oldest light in the universe, released 380,000 years after the Big Bang, holds the recipe of the cosmos in its tiny ripples.
x: Discovery # In 1964–65 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs could not get rid of a faint hiss in their horn antenna, even after cleaning out pigeon droppings. It came from every direction: the afterglow of the Big Bang, predicted by Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman in 1948. They won the 1978 Nobel Prize. What it shows # A temperature of 2.725 K , the most perfect blackbody spectrum in nature (COBE, 1992, Nobel 2006). Ripples of about 1 part in 100,000 : the seeds of every galaxy. The pattern of those ripples (‘acoustic peaks’) reveals the universe’s age (13.8 billion years), geometry (flat), and contents (~5% ordinary matter, ~27% dark matter, ~68% dark energy), as measured by Planck (2009–13). Missions # Mission Years Achievement COBE 1989–93 Blackbody spectrum; first ripples WMAP 2001–10 Precise age and composition Planck 2009–13 Definitive all-sky map ACT, SPT Ground Fine-scale detail and lensing Simons Observatory, LiteBIRD Now / 2030s Search for inflation’s gravitational-wave signature Anomalies # A large ‘Cold Spot’ and slight alignments of the largest patterns (‘axis of evil’) are debated. Most cosmologists consider them statistical flukes, but they are watched closely.

t: Cosmic Dawn: The First Stars and Galaxies
d: After 380,000 years of glow came the cosmic dark ages, then the first stars lit up the universe. JWST now sees galaxies from less than 300 million years after the Big Bang.
x: Record for the most distant galaxy (redshift z) 10.7 2012 11.1 2016 GN-z11 13.2 2022 14.3 2024 JADES-z14 14.44 2025 MoM-z14 Source: HST/JWST discoveries The dark ages (380,000 – ~100 million years) # After the CMB was released the universe went dark. There were no stars, only cooling hydrogen and helium gas and invisible dark matter slowly clumping under gravity. The first stars (Population III) # Within roughly 100–200 million years, gas falling into dark-matter clumps became dense enough to ignite fusion. The first stars contained only hydrogen and helium. They are thought to have been huge (tens to hundreds of Suns), very hot and short-lived , dying in supernovae that forged the first heavy elements. No Population III star has yet been confirmed, though JWST is searching. Reionisation # Ultraviolet light from early stars and galaxies stripped electrons from the neutral hydrogen filling space, ‘reionising’ the universe by about 1 billion years after the Big Bang. JWST’s surprise # Record-breaking early galaxies JADES-GS-z14-0 : confirmed at redshift 14.3 in 2024. MoM-z14 : confirmed at z = 14.44 , about 280 million years after the Big Bang, the current record. See Naidu et al. 2026 . Many early galaxies are brighter and more numerous than models predicted , and some host surprisingly massive black holes. These findings do not overturn the Big Bang, but they challenge how fast stars and black holes could form. Proposed explanations include more efficient star formation, a different stellar mass mix, or black holes that started heavy (‘direct collapse’). From first galaxies to today # Small galaxies merged into larger ones. The Milky Way’s oldest stars are ~13 billion years old, and its disk formed later. Star formation across the universe peaked about 10 billion years ago (‘cosmic noon’) and has been declining since. Next: How big is the universe?

t: How Big Is the Universe? From the Earth to the Cosmic Horizon
d: A journey of scale, from the Earth–Moon distance to the observable universe 93 billion light-years across, and what 'vast and empty' really means.
x: The Hubble tension: measurements of H₀ (km/s/Mpc) SH0ES (Cepheids + SNe) SH0ES (Cepheids + SNe) 73 CCHP (TRGB/JAGB, 2025) CCHP (TRGB/JAGB, 2025) 70.4 Planck CMB (ΛCDM) Planck CMB (ΛCDM) 67.4 Source: Riess et al.; Freedman et al. 2025; Planck 2018 A ladder of distances # Step Distance Light-travel time Earth to Moon 384,400 km 1.3 seconds Earth to Sun (1 AU) 150 million km 8.3 minutes Sun to Neptune 30 AU ~4 hours Voyager 1 (Nov 2026) ~173 AU 1 light-day , the first human object this far Oort Cloud outer edge ~100,000 AU ~1.5 years Nearest star (Proxima Centauri) 4.24 light-years 4.24 years Across the Milky Way ~100,000 light-years — Andromeda Galaxy 2.5 million light-years — Laniakea Supercluster ~520 million light-years across — Observable universe ~93 billion light-years across — The observable universe is larger than 13.8 billion light-years in radius because space has expanded while the light was travelling: the most distant regions we see are now ~46 billion light-years away. How we measure: the cosmic distance ladder # Radar and spacecraft within the solar system. Parallax : the shift of nearby stars as Earth orbits; Gaia measured ~2 billion stars. Standard candles : Cepheid variables, the tip of the red giant branch, and Type Ia supernovae. Redshift : Hubble’s law converts recession speed into distance. Disagreement between rungs of this ladder is at the heart of the Hubble tension . How empty is space? # If the Sun were a grapefruit in London, Proxima Centauri would be another grapefruit in Moscow. The interstellar medium averages about 1 atom per cubic centimetre ; intergalactic space about 1 atom per cubic metre , emptier than any lab vacuum. Cosmic voids such as the Boötes Void span ~330 million light-years with very few galaxies. See Cosmic void . Even ‘empty’ space carries the CMB, neutrinos, magnetic fields, dark matter, dark energy and quantum vacuum fluctuations. Is the universe infinite? # We don’t know. Measurements show space is flat to within ~0.4%, which is consistent with an infinite universe or a finite one far larger than we can see.

t: Dark Matter and Dark Energy: The 95% We Can't See
d: Ordinary matter is under 5% of the universe. The rest is dark matter (~27%) and dark energy (~68%), and in 2025 DESI hinted that dark energy may be changing.
x: What the universe is made of Dark energy: 68 Dark matter: 27 Ordinary matter: 5 100 ■ Dark energy — 68 (68%) ■ Dark matter — 27 (27%) ■ Ordinary matter — 5 (5%) Percent of total energy density (Planck 2018). Dark matter # Discovery: Fritz Zwicky (1933) found galaxies in the Coma cluster moving too fast; Vera Rubin and Kent Ford (1970s) showed spiral galaxies rotate too fast at their edges. Evidence today: gravitational lensing, the Bullet Cluster (mass separated from hot gas), CMB fluctuation patterns, and the growth of cosmic structure. Candidates: WIMPs (not yet found in direct-detection experiments such as LZ), axions, sterile neutrinos and primordial black holes. Modified-gravity theories such as MOND explain some galaxy data but struggle with clusters and the CMB. Dark energy # In 1998 two teams measuring Type Ia supernovae found the expansion of the universe is accelerating (Nobel Prize 2011). The simplest explanation is Einstein’s cosmological constant, the energy of empty space. Is dark energy evolving? The DESI collaboration’s 2025 DR2 baryon-acoustic-oscillation results, combined with supernovae and the CMB, prefer a dark energy that weakens over time at 2.8–4.2σ , depending on which supernova sample is used. That is suggestive but below the 5σ discovery threshold. Euclid and Rubin will test it. See DESI 2025 analysis . Why it matters # Dark energy decides the fate of the universe; dark matter decides how galaxies formed. Together they are the biggest unsolved problem in physics. See The fate of the universe .

d: Heat death, Big Rip, Big Crunch or something stranger? What happens over the next trillions of years depends on dark energy.
x: The near future (billions of years) # ~1 billion years: the brightening Sun boils away Earth’s oceans. ~4–5 billion years: the Milky Way and Andromeda may merge into one elliptical galaxy (‘Milkomeda’). A 2025 study put the chance of a merger within 10 billion years at about 50%. ~5 billion years: the Sun becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf. The far future # Era When What happens Stelliferous era Now – ~100 trillion years Stars keep forming until gas runs out; red dwarfs shine for trillions of years. Degenerate era ~10¹⁴ – 10⁴⁰ years Only white dwarfs, neutron stars, brown dwarfs and black holes remain; protons may decay. Black hole era ~10⁴⁰ – 10¹⁰⁰ years Black holes dominate, slowly evaporating via Hawking radiation. Dark era >10¹⁰⁰ years A cold, dilute sea of photons and particles. Possible endings # Heat death (Big Freeze): with a constant dark energy, expansion continues for ever and the universe reaches maximum entropy. This is the leading expectation. Big Rip: if dark energy grows stronger (‘phantom’ energy), it would eventually tear apart galaxies, stars and atoms. Big Crunch: if dark energy weakens and reverses, expansion could stop and collapse. DESI’s hint of weakening dark energy has revived interest in this. Vacuum decay: if the Higgs field sits in a ‘false vacuum’, a bubble of lower energy could spread at light speed. It is possible in theory and extremely unlikely on any relevant timescale.

d: From collapsing gas clouds to white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes, a star's mass decides its whole life story.
x: Birth: from nebula to protostar # Stars form in cold molecular clouds. A disturbance, such as a nearby supernova shock or galactic collision, makes a dense clump collapse. It spins up and flattens into a disk around a hot protostar. When the core reaches ~10 million K, hydrogen fusion ignites and a star is born. Leftover disk material can form planets. Life: the main sequence # The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots brightness against temperature. Stars spend ~90% of their lives on the main sequence , fusing hydrogen. Mass (Suns) Lifetime Fate 0.08–0.5 (red dwarf) Trillions of years Fades to a white dwarf (none has yet finished) 0.5–8 (Sun-like) ~10 billion years for the Sun Red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf 8–25 ~10–50 million years Red supergiant → core-collapse supernova → neutron star >25 A few million years Supernova or direct collapse → black hole Death # Sun-like stars swell into red giants, fuse helium into carbon and oxygen, shed their outer layers as a glowing planetary nebula , and leave a white dwarf . Massive stars build an onion of shells (hydrogen, helium, carbon, neon, oxygen, silicon) around an iron core. Iron fusion absorbs energy, so the core collapses in under a second, triggering a supernova and leaving a neutron star or black hole . We are made of star stuff # Carbon in your cells, oxygen you breathe and calcium in your bones were forged in stars. Iron came from supernovae, and much of the gold and platinum on Earth from neutron-star mergers ( kilonovae ).

d: The two ways stars explode, the famous supernovae in history, and why they matter for life, cosmology and the elements.
x: A supernova can briefly outshine its whole galaxy, releasing as much energy as the Sun will in its entire life. Two main types # Type Cause Leaves behind Use Core-collapse (II, Ib, Ic) Iron core of a >8-Sun star collapses Neutron star or black hole Forges and spreads oxygen, silicon, calcium Thermonuclear (Ia) White dwarf pushed over ~1.4 Suns ignites Nothing ‘Standard candles’ that revealed dark energy Supernovae in history # 1006 CE : the brightest stellar event ever recorded, seen worldwide. 1054 CE : recorded by Chinese astronomers; its remnant is the Crab Nebula . 1572 : Tycho Brahe’s supernova showed that the heavens change. 1604 : Kepler’s supernova, the last seen in the Milky Way. 1987 : SN 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Two dozen neutrinos detected hours before the light confirmed the core-collapse theory, and JWST found its neutron star in 2024. 2023 : SN 2023ixf in the Pinwheel Galaxy, the closest in a decade. Next nearby candidates # Betelgeuse (550 light-years) will explode sometime in the next ~100,000 years and be visible in daylight, but it is too far to harm Earth. A supernova would need to be within ~50 light-years to damage the ozone layer. Why they matter # They spread the elements needed for planets and life. Shock waves trigger new star formation (possibly including the Sun’s). Iron-60 in deep-sea sediments shows nearby supernovae showered Earth ~2–3 million years ago.

t: Dead Stars: White Dwarfs, Neutron Stars, Pulsars and Magnetars
d: The compact corpses of stars hold matter at densities found nowhere else, from diamond-like white dwarfs to neutron stars where a teaspoon weighs a billion tonnes.
x: White dwarfs # The cores of Sun-like stars: about the Sun’s mass squeezed into an Earth-sized ball, held up by electron degeneracy pressure . Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar (from Lahore, then British India) calculated in 1930 that none can exceed ~1.4 solar masses, the Chandrasekhar limit (Nobel Prize 1983). As they cool, their carbon-oxygen interiors crystallise . See White dwarf . Neutron stars # Collapsed cores of massive stars, ~20 km across but 1.2–2.3 times the Sun’s mass. Protons and electrons are crushed into neutrons. Surface gravity is ~100 billion times Earth’s, and mountains are millimetres high. Pulsars # Spinning neutron stars sweeping beams across Earth. Jocelyn Bell Burnell found the first in 1967 as a research student. Pulsars are such precise clocks that: - the Hulse–Taylor binary pulsar gave the first indirect evidence of gravitational waves (Nobel 1993); - pulsar timing arrays (including India’s GMRT and InPTA) detected a gravitational-wave background in 2023. Magnetars # Neutron stars with magnetic fields ~10¹⁵ gauss, a thousand trillion times Earth’s. Starquakes release giant flares; in 2020 a Milky Way magnetar produced a fast radio burst . Black dwarfs # When a white dwarf has fully cooled it becomes a black dwarf. The universe isn’t old enough for any to exist yet.

d: 'Dwarf' covers very different objects: ordinary small stars, failed stars, and stellar corpses. Here is how to tell them apart.

Red dwarfs (M): 76 Orange (K): 12 Yellow (G, like the Sun): 7.6 White (F): 3 Hot blue-white (A, B, O): 1.4 100.0 ■ Red dwarfs (M) — 76 (76%) ■ Orange (K) — 12 (12%) ■ Yellow (G, like the Sun) — 7.6 (8%) ■ White (F) — 3 (3%) ■ Hot blue-white (A, B, O) — 1.4 (1%) Approximate share of main-sequence stars near the Sun. Red dwarfs and life # Red dwarfs are so common that most Earth-sized planets in habitable zones probably orbit them. But they flare violently when young and planets close to them may be tidally locked, with one side always facing the star. JWST is testing whether planets like TRAPPIST-1e can keep atmospheres. Brown dwarfs # Between ~13 and ~80 Jupiter masses. They glow from heat left over from formation and cool for ever. The coldest, WISE 0855−0714 , is below the freezing point of water and has water-ice clouds. Some free-floating ‘rogue planets’ blur the line between planets and brown dwarfs.

t: Star Patterns: Constellations, Asterisms and Nakshatras
d: How cultures connected the stars, the 88 official constellations, why patterns slowly change, and how ancient Indian astronomy divided the sky.
x: Constellations versus asterisms # The International Astronomical Union recognises 88 constellations (fixed in 1922, boundaries drawn by Eugène Delporte in 1930) that together tile the entire sky. Browse them all in the Constellations catalog. Asterisms are popular patterns that are not official constellations: the Big Dipper (Saptarishi), the Summer Triangle , Orion’s Belt, the Teapot in Sagittarius. Stars in a pattern aren’t neighbours # Stars in a constellation lie at very different distances. In Orion, Betelgeuse is ~550 light-years away and Rigel ~860. They only line up from our viewpoint. The sky slowly changes # Precession: Earth’s axis wobbles every ~26,000 years, so the pole star changes: Thuban (Draco) for the pyramid builders, Polaris now, Vega in ~12,000 years. This shifted the zodiac relative to the seasons. Proper motion: stars move. In ~50,000 years the Big Dipper will look noticeably bent. Indian astronomy # The ecliptic is divided into 27 (or 28) nakshatras , lunar mansions such as Krittika (the Pleiades) and Rohini (Aldebaran). Aryabhata (499 CE) proposed that Earth rotates on its axis and explained eclipses by shadows. Varahamihira and Brahmagupta advanced mathematical astronomy. The Jantar Mantar observatories of Sawai Jai Singh II (1720s–30s) measured time and positions with giant masonry instruments. Navigation and culture # Polynesian navigators used rising and setting points of stars; Indigenous Australians read ‘dark constellations’ such as the Emu in the Sky in the dust lanes of the Milky Way; sailors everywhere used Polaris and the Southern Cross.

d: Our star powers life but also hurls flares and storms at Earth. Solar Cycle 25 peaked in October 2024, and Parker Solar Probe now flies through the Sun's atmosphere.

The solar cycle # Sunspots rise and fall over ~11 years as the magnetic field flips. Solar Cycle 25 reached its maximum in October 2024 (smoothed sunspot number ~161), stronger than forecast. The Carrington Event (1859) set telegraph lines on fire; a similar storm today could damage power grids and satellites. Solar Orbiter (ESA–NASA) photographed the Sun’s poles for the first time (2025). Aditya-L1 (ISRO, 2023) watches the Sun continuously from the L1 point. More: Research: heliophysics .

d: Event horizons, singularities, spaghettification, time dilation and spin, explained step by step, with the evidence that black holes are real.
x: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light. Anatomy of a black hole # Part What it is Singularity Where general relativity predicts infinite density; a sign that a quantum theory of gravity is needed. Event horizon The point of no return. For a non-spinning black hole its radius is the Schwarzschild radius: ~3 km per solar mass. Photon sphere At 1.5× the horizon radius, light can orbit the black hole. ISCO The innermost stable circular orbit, the inner edge of most accretion disks. Accretion disk Gas spiralling in, heated to millions of degrees; it can outshine whole galaxies (quasars). Jets Beams of particles launched near light speed by magnetic fields and spin. What would happen if you fell in? # Tidal forces stretch you lengthwise ( spaghettification ). Near a small black hole this kills you before the horizon; near a supermassive one you could cross the horizon intact. Time dilation: a distant observer sees you slow down and redden, never quite crossing; you cross without noticing anything special. Inside, all paths lead to the singularity. Types # Type Mass Example Stellar 3–100 Suns Cygnus X-1, Gaia BH3 Intermediate 100–100,000 Suns Omega Centauri (2024 evidence) Supermassive Millions to billions of Suns Sgr A* , M87* Primordial Any (hypothetical) Not yet found How we know they exist # X-ray binaries (Cygnus X-1, 1971). Stars orbiting Sgr A* , tracked for 30 years by Reinhard Genzel’s and Andrea Ghez’s teams (Nobel 2020, shared with Roger Penrose). Gravitational waves from merging black holes (since 2015). See Gravitational waves . Event Horizon Telescope images of M87 (2019) and Sgr A (2022), showing the shadow ringed by light. Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners # Replace the Sun with a black hole of the same mass and Earth’s orbit would not change. Black holes only ‘suck’ when you get close. Information and Hawking radiation # Stephen Hawking showed (1974) that black holes should slowly evaporate. If they do, what happens to the information about what fell in? This information paradox remains a central puzzle linking gravity and quantum mechanics.

d: Einstein predicted ripples in spacetime in 1916. A century later LIGO heard two black holes merge, opening a new way to observe the cosmos.

t: White Holes and Wormholes: Science or Science Fiction?
d: Both appear as solutions of Einstein's equations, but neither has ever been observed. Here is what the maths says, the problems, and the ideas physicists still take seriously.
x: Theoretical only There is no observational evidence for white holes or traversable wormholes. Everything on this page is theory. White holes # A white hole is the time-reverse of a black hole: nothing can enter its horizon, but matter and light can only come out. It appears in the full (‘maximally extended’) Schwarzschild solution of general relativity, found by Martin Kruskal and George Szekeres in 1960. Problems: it would be extremely unstable. Any matter falling toward it would pile up and likely collapse it into a black hole. It also seems to violate the second law of thermodynamics. Speculative ideas: loop quantum gravity models suggest black holes might ‘bounce’ into white holes at the end of their lives; some have proposed the Big Bang itself was white-hole-like. Some have even suggested that unusual, short gamma-ray bursts could be white holes; there is no support for this. Wormholes # A wormhole (Einstein–Rosen bridge, 1935) connects two distant regions of spacetime through a ‘throat’. The original Einstein–Rosen bridge pinches off too fast for anything, even light, to pass through. Kip Thorne and Michael Morris (1988) showed that a traversable wormhole would need exotic matter with negative energy to hold it open. Tiny negative energies exist (the Casimir effect), but nowhere near enough. Wormholes could in principle act as time machines, which raises paradoxes; Hawking’s chronology protection conjecture suggests physics forbids this. ER = EPR: Juan Maldacena and Leonard Susskind (2013) proposed that quantum entanglement and wormholes may be two sides of the same thing. A 2022 ‘wormhole on a quantum chip’ experiment simulated a toy model; it did not create a real wormhole. In fiction # Interstellar (2014) used Kip Thorne’s equations to render its wormhole and black hole Gargantua, producing a scientifically grounded image of a black hole years before the Event Horizon Telescope.

t: Cosmic Collisions: From Asteroid Impacts to Galaxy Mergers
d: Collisions shape everything, from the Moon's birth and the dinosaurs' extinction to merging black holes and colliding galaxy clusters.
x: Scale Example Result Planet formation Theia hitting the young Earth ~4.5 billion years ago Formed the Moon Asteroid impacts Chicxulub , 66 million years ago Mass extinction, end of the dinosaurs Comet into a planet Shoemaker-Levy 9 into Jupiter, 1994 Earth-sized dark scars on Jupiter Spacecraft into an asteroid DART into Dimorphos, 2022 Orbit shortened by 33 minutes, first planetary-defence test Star mergers V1309 Scorpii , 2008 A ‘red nova’ Neutron stars GW170817 , 2017 A kilonova that forged gold and platinum Black holes GW150914 , 2015 Three Suns’ worth of energy released as gravitational waves Galaxies Antennae Galaxies ; Milky Way and Andromeda in the future Starbursts, new elliptical galaxies Galaxy clusters Bullet Cluster , El Gordo Key evidence for dark matter Planetary defence # NASA, ESA and others track near-Earth objects. Asteroid Apophis will pass within ~32,000 km of Earth on 13 April 2029 (no risk of impact). 2024 YR4 briefly had a ~3% impact probability for 2032 before being ruled out. NASA’s NEO Surveyor (launch ~2027) and the Rubin Observatory will find many more. Why stars in colliding galaxies rarely hit # Stars are tiny compared with the gaps between them. When the Milky Way and Andromeda merge, almost no stars will collide, but gas clouds will crash together and trigger bursts of new stars.

t: How Planets and the Solar System Formed
d: From a collapsing cloud 4.6 billion years ago to eight planets, a few dwarf planets and trillions of comets: the nebular theory and its surprises.
x: Planet radius compared with Earth Jupiter Jupiter 10.97× Saturn Saturn 9.14× Uranus Uranus 3.98× Neptune Neptune 3.86× Earth Earth 1× Venus Venus 0.95× Mars Mars 0.53× Mercury Mercury 0.38× Pluto Pluto 0.19× Source: NASA planetary fact sheets The nebular theory # ~4.6 billion years ago a cloud of gas and dust collapsed, possibly triggered by a nearby supernova (short-lived isotopes like aluminium-26 in meteorites hint at this). The cloud spun up into a flat protoplanetary disk around the young Sun. ALMA now images such disks around other stars, with gaps carved by forming planets. Dust grains stuck together into pebbles, then kilometre-sized planetesimals , then protoplanets. Inside the snow line (~2.7 AU) only rock and metal could condense, making small rocky planets. Beyond it, ice was plentiful, so cores grew big enough to grab hydrogen and helium: the gas giants. Giant impacts finished the rocky planets; one created the Moon. The planets migrated # The Nice model and Grand Tack propose that Jupiter and Saturn wandered, scattering asteroids and comets, possibly causing the Late Heavy Bombardment and delivering water to Earth. Leftovers # Asteroid belt: debris Jupiter prevented from forming a planet. Kuiper Belt: icy bodies beyond Neptune, including Pluto and Arrokoth. Oort Cloud: a vast shell of comets reaching perhaps 100,000 AU. Other solar systems are different # Exoplanet discoveries showed that our system is not typical: hot Jupiters, super-Earths and sub-Neptunes (missing here) are common. See Types of planets .

d: Over 6,000 exoplanets are now confirmed. They include hot Jupiters, super-Earths, sub-Neptunes, lava worlds, water worlds, puffy planets, circumbinary 'Tatooines' and rogue planets with no star.

t: How We Find Planets Around Other Stars
d: Transits, wobbles, microlensing, direct imaging and pulsar timing, with how each works and what it finds best.
x: Method How it works Best at Share of discoveries Transit A planet crossing its star dims it slightly (Earth dims the Sun by 0.008%) Short-period planets; gives radius and atmosphere via spectroscopy ~75% Radial velocity The star wobbles, shifting its spectrum (Doppler effect) Massive planets near their stars; gives minimum mass ~18% Microlensing A foreground star and planet bend a background star’s light Cold planets far from their stars; rogue planets ~4% Direct imaging Block the starlight with a coronagraph and photograph the planet Young, hot giants on wide orbits ~1% Timing Pulsar or eclipse timing variations Pulsar planets <1% Astrometry The star’s tiny sideways motion Gaia’s long-period giants Growing Try it # Use the Transit Lab to see how planet size changes the light curve. Key missions # Kepler (2009–18), TESS (2018–), JWST (atmospheres), CHEOPS, Gaia (astrometry), Roman Space Telescope (launched 2026, microlensing survey), PLATO (ESA, ~2026–27), and the proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory (2040s) to image Earth twins. Reading an atmosphere # When starlight passes through a planet’s atmosphere during transit, molecules absorb particular colours. JWST has detected water, CO₂, methane, sulfur dioxide and more, and is testing claims like dimethyl sulfide on K2-18 b .

t: Space Rocks: Meteors, Meteorites, Asteroids and Comets
d: The difference between a meteor and a meteorite, the main rock types that fall from space, and what they tell us about the birth of the solar system.
x: Words that get mixed up # Term Meaning Meteoroid A small rock or dust grain in space Meteor The streak of light when a meteoroid burns up in the atmosphere (‘shooting star’) Meteorite A piece that survives and lands Asteroid A rocky or metallic body, metres to hundreds of km across, mostly between Mars and Jupiter Comet An icy body that grows a glowing coma and tails near the Sun Fireball / bolide An exceptionally bright meteor, sometimes exploding (Chelyabinsk 2013) Kinds of meteorites # Browse them in the Space Rocks catalog. Stony (~94%) : chondrites with chondrules older than the planets, and carbonaceous chondrites rich in water and organics. Iron (~5%) : cores of shattered protoplanets. Stony-iron (~1%) : pallasites with olivine gems in metal. Planetary : ~400 from Mars and ~700 from the Moon. Meteor showers # Earth crosses streams of comet dust: the Perseids (August, Comet Swift–Tuttle), Geminids (December, asteroid 3200 Phaethon) and Leonids (November, Comet Tempel–Tuttle). Samples brought home # Apollo and Luna (Moon), Chang’e 5 and 6 (Moon, including the far side), Stardust (comet dust), Hayabusa and Hayabusa2 (asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu), OSIRIS-REx (Bennu, whose samples contain amino acids and all five nucleobases of DNA and RNA). Tianwen-2 is now sampling asteroid Kamoʻoalewa. India’s impact crater # Lonar Lake in Maharashtra is a ~1.8 km crater in basalt, a rare analogue for impacts on the Moon and Mars.

t: Is There Life Out There? Habitability and Biosignatures
d: Where life could exist beyond Earth, from Mars and icy moons to exoplanets, how scientists would recognise it, and the claims that remain unconfirmed.
x: What life needs (as far as we know) # Liquid water, an energy source (sunlight or chemistry), and elements such as carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur. Deep-sea vents show life can run on chemistry alone. The best places to look # World Why Status Mars Ancient lakes and rivers; organic molecules Perseverance’s 2025 ‘potential biosignature’ at Sapphire Canyon is unconfirmed; sample return was cancelled in 2026 Europa Salty ocean under ice Europa Clipper arrives 2030 Enceladus Plumes containing water, salts, organics and phosphorus Prime target for a future orbiter-lander Titan Methane lakes and a buried water ocean Dragonfly launches ~2028 Venus clouds Temperate cloud layer Phosphine claim disputed Exoplanets Billions of habitable-zone planets JWST probing TRAPPIST-1 and K2-18 b How we’d know: confidence levels # Scientists use a ladder of evidence (NASA’s CoLD scale, Green et al. 2021) from ‘signal detected’ up to ‘confirmed life’. Every current claim is on the lower rungs. See Research: biosignatures and K2-18 b debate . SETI and the Fermi paradox # Radio searches (Breakthrough Listen, SETI Institute) have found no technosignatures. If life is common, why haven’t we seen anyone? Possible answers range from ‘they are too far’ to ‘intelligent life is extraordinarily rare’.

t: The Telescope: From Galileo's Spyglass to JWST
d: 400 years of seeing farther, from the first lens telescopes of 1608–09 to radio dishes, gravitational-wave detectors and JWST.
x: Before telescopes # Naked-eye astronomers built precise instruments: Hipparchus’s star catalogue (~150 BCE), Ulugh Beg’s Samarkand observatory (1420s), Tycho Brahe’s measurements (1570s–90s) that Kepler used to discover elliptical orbits, and Jai Singh II’s Jantar Mantar observatories in India (1720s–30s). The first telescopes # 1608: Dutch spectacle-maker Hans Lippershey applied for a patent on a ‘device for seeing far’. 1609–10: Galileo Galilei built his own (~20×) and found Jupiter’s four big moons, the phases of Venus, mountains on the Moon and countless stars in the Milky Way, evidence that helped overturn the Earth-centred universe. 1611: Kepler designed a better refractor with two convex lenses. 1668: Isaac Newton built the first practical reflecting telescope, using a mirror to avoid colour fringes. Bigger and bigger # Year Telescope Discovery 1781 Herschel’s reflector Uranus, the first planet found by telescope 1845 Leviathan of Parsonstown Spiral ‘nebulae’ (galaxies) 1917 Hooker 2.5 m Hubble shows galaxies are separate and the universe expands 1948 Hale 5 m Quasars, stellar populations 1993 Keck 10 m Segmented mirrors, adaptive optics 2029 (planned) ELT 39 m Earth-like exoplanet atmospheres Beyond visible light # Radio: Karl Jansky (1932) heard the Milky Way; radio telescopes found pulsars, quasars and the CMB. India’s GMRT near Pune is one of the largest low-frequency arrays. Space telescopes: Hubble (1990), Chandra (X-ray), Spitzer and JWST (infrared, 2021), Gaia, Euclid, and Roman (launched August 2026). New messengers: neutrinos (IceCube), gravitational waves (LIGO, with LIGO-India under construction). Browse the full Telescopes catalog.

t: The Space Race and the Moon Landings
d: From Sputnik in 1957 to Apollo 17 in 1972, and now Artemis: how humans first left Earth and walked on another world.
x: Farthest humans from Earth (km) 420 ISS orbit 377,000 Apollo 8 (1968) 400,171 Apollo 13 (1970) 406,771 Artemis II (2026) Source: NASA The race # 1957 : Sputnik 1 , the first satellite; Sputnik 2 carries Laika. 1958 : NASA is founded; Explorer 1 finds the Van Allen belts. 1961 : Yuri Gagarin becomes the first human in space; Alan Shepard follows; Kennedy commits to the Moon. 1963 : Valentina Tereshkova , the first woman in space. 1965 : Alexei Leonov makes the first spacewalk. 1966 : Luna 9 makes the first soft landing on the Moon. 1967 : The Apollo 1 fire kills three astronauts. 1968 : Apollo 8 orbits the Moon and photographs 'Earthrise'. 20 Jul 1969 : Apollo 11 , Armstrong and Aldrin walk on the Moon. 1970 : Apollo 13's crew survives an explosion. 1972 : Apollo 17 , the last crewed landing; 12 people have walked on the Moon. The 12 moonwalkers # See them all in the People & Animals catalog. Apollo brought back 382 kg of Moon rock that revealed the Moon formed from a giant impact. Returning: Artemis # Artemis I (2022): uncrewed test around the Moon. Artemis II (1–10 April 2026): Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen flew around the Moon, the first crew beyond low Earth orbit since 1972, setting a human distance record of 406,771 km. Artemis III was reshaped in 2026 into an Earth-orbit docking test with landers (~mid-2027); the first new landing is targeted for Artemis IV (~2028) . China plans crewed landings by 2030, and India plans a crewed Moon landing by 2040. Why go back? # Water ice in permanently shadowed craters near the south pole could supply drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel. Chandrayaan-1’s instruments helped confirm water on the Moon, and Chandrayaan-3 landed near the south pole in 2023.

d: Newton's third law, the rocket equation, why orbit is 'falling and missing', escape velocity, transfer orbits and the special places in space (Lagrange points).
x: Rockets # A rocket pushes exhaust backward and is pushed forward (Newton’s third law); it doesn’t need air to push against. The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation (1903) shows why rockets are mostly fuel: speed gained depends on exhaust velocity and the logarithm of the starting-to-final mass ratio. That is why rockets use stages and why reusability (Falcon 9, Starship) has slashed costs. Orbits are falling and missing # Throw a ball faster and it lands farther away. At ~7.8 km/s (about 28,000 km/h) at 400 km altitude, the ground curves away as fast as you fall: you are in orbit. Astronauts float because they and the station fall together, not because gravity is absent (it’s ~90% of surface gravity at the ISS). Orbit Altitude Uses Low Earth orbit (LEO) 160–2,000 km ISS, Tiangong, Starlink, Earth observation Sun-synchronous ~600–800 km Imaging at the same local time Medium Earth orbit ~20,000 km GPS, Galileo navigation Geostationary (GEO) 35,786 km Communications, weather (INSAT/GSAT); satellites hover over one spot Lagrange points e.g. L1/L2, 1.5 million km Aditya-L1 (L1), JWST and Gaia (L2) Getting to other worlds # Escape velocity from Earth is 11.2 km/s. A Hohmann transfer is the most fuel-efficient path between two orbits; to Mars it takes ~7–9 months and launch windows open every ~26 months. Gravity assists steal momentum from planets (Voyager’s ‘grand tour’, Europa Clipper’s Earth flyby in December 2026). Try the Orbital Mechanics Lab . Space debris # Over 30,000 tracked objects orbit Earth. Collisions could trigger a cascade (the Kessler syndrome). In 2019 India tested an anti-satellite missile (Mission Shakti) at low altitude so that most debris would re-enter quickly.

d: What spaceflight does to the body, the animals that went first, records for time in space, and how astronauts live on the ISS.
x: Animals went first # Fruit flies (1947), monkeys (1949), dogs ( Laika , 1957, the first to orbit; Belka and Strelka , 1960, the first to return), chimpanzee Ham (1961), Félicette the cat (1963), tortoises around the Moon (Zond 5, 1968), spiders, fish, jellyfish, mice and tardigrades, which survived open space. See the People & Animals catalog. What space does to the body # Effect Cause Countermeasure Bone loss (~1–1.5% per month) No load on bones ~2 hours of exercise daily Muscle loss Microgravity Resistance machines Fluid shift, ‘puffy face’, vision changes (SANS) Fluids move to the head Under study Radiation Cosmic rays, solar storms Shielding, storm shelters Space motion sickness Confused inner ear Adapts in days Taller by up to ~5 cm Spine decompresses Returns on landing NASA’s Twins Study (Scott and Mark Kelly, 2015–16) showed most changes reverse after a year in space. Records # Longest single flight: Valeri Polyakov , 437 days on Mir (1994–95). Most cumulative time: Oleg Kononenko , over 1,000 days (2024). Farthest from Earth: the Artemis II crew, 406,771 km (April 2026). India in human spaceflight # Rakesh Sharma flew in 1984. Shubhanshu Shukla became the first Indian aboard the ISS on Axiom-4 (2025). ISRO’s Gaganyaan programme plans the uncrewed G1 flight, then India’s first crewed launch in 2027.

d: From launching rocket parts by bicycle in the 1960s to landing near the Moon's south pole, studying the Sun, and preparing Gaganyaan.
x: 1963 : First sounding rocket launched from Thumba, Kerala; parts carried by bicycle and bullock cart. 1969 : ISRO founded under Vikram Sarabhai. 1975 : Aryabhata , India's first satellite. 1980 : SLV-3 puts Rohini into orbit; India becomes a launching nation. 1984 : Rakesh Sharma flies to Salyut 7. 1993 : PSLV debuts, later becoming one of the most reliable rockets. 2008 : Chandrayaan-1 ; its instruments help confirm water on the Moon. 2014 : Mangalyaan reaches Mars orbit on the first attempt. 2015 : AstroSat , India's first space observatory. 2017 : PSLV-C37 launches a record 104 satellites. 2019 : Chandrayaan-2's orbiter succeeds; the lander crashes. 2023 : Chandrayaan-3 lands near the lunar south pole (23 August, now National Space Day); Aditya-L1 launches to study the Sun. 2025 : NISAR (NASA–ISRO radar) launches; Shubhanshu Shukla visits the ISS; SpaDeX demonstrates docking. 2026 : Gaganyaan separation tests complete; uncrewed G1 flight targeted. The private sector (Skyroot, Agnikul) launched India’s first private rockets in 2022 and 2024.

t: Research Now: Cosmology, the Hubble Tension and Dark Energy
d: The latest numbers and debates: H₀ measurements, DESI's evolving dark energy hint and JWST's early universe.
x: Status date: November 15, 2026. Concepts # Cosmic microwave background (CMB) Light released ~380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe cooled enough for atoms to form. Its tiny temperature ripples (~1 part in 100,000) seeded all later structure. ΛCDM energy budget (Planck 2018) Dark energy ≈ 68.5%, dark matter ≈ 26.5%, ordinary (baryonic) matter ≈ 4.9%. Redshift z Expansion stretches light: 1 + z = (size of universe now) / (size when the light left). Higher z means further back in time. Baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) Sound waves in the early plasma left a preferred spacing (~150 Mpc today) between galaxies. Measuring it at many redshifts gives a “standard ruler” for the expansion history. Live Debate 1: Is dark energy changing? # What DESI reported (2025-03-19, DR2) Three years of data covering nearly 15 million galaxies and quasars, the largest 3D map yet. DESI on its own is consistent with ΛCDM. Combined with CMB and supernova data, it prefers an evolving dark energy at 2.8–4.2σ , depending on which supernova sample is used. How to read the plot ( png/dark_energy_evolution_generated.png ) Uses the common w0–wa parameterisation: w(a) = w0 + wa(1 − a). With w0 ≈ −0.75, wa ≈ −0.86, dark-energy density rises slightly then falls as you look back. In other words, today’s dark energy would be weaker than its recent peak. The curve is illustrative, not a fit I made. Why caution 5σ is the discovery threshold, and the signal depends on how supernova datasets are calibrated. Live Debate 2: The Hubble tension # Early-universe inference (CMB + ΛCDM) gives H0 ≈ 67 km/s/Mpc. Local distance-ladder measurements (Cepheids + Type Ia supernovae) give ≈ 73 km/s/Mpc. SH0ES (Riess et al.): JWST re-observed Cepheids, more than 1,000 across several hosts, with ~2% distance precision. Crowding errors in Hubble photometry are now hard to blame. Values: ~73.2, and 72.6 cross-checked with carbon stars and red giants. CCHP (Freedman et al., ApJ 2025): TRGB + JWST gives 70.39 km/s/Mpc , which the team says is consistent with ΛCDM. Their own Cepheid subset gives 72.04. Critics (e.g. Riess, Scolnic) argue the sample is small and selected from the tail, and that 70.4 sits in the middle of the tension rather than resolving it. My read: the tension is now mostly about which local calibrator to trust (Cepheids vs TRGB/JAGB), not about Hubble photometry. Independent methods (lensing time delays, TDCOSMO; gravitational-wave sirens) are the tie-breakers. Either there is unrecognised systematic error, or there is new physics. Evolving dark energy alone does not obviously fix it. Live Debate 3: Too many early galaxies? # MoM-z14 : spectroscopically confirmed at z = 14.44 (~280 Myr after the Big Bang), about 240 light-years across. Paper: Naidu et al., Open Journal of Astrophysics , 2026. The bright z > 10 population is >100× more abundant than pre-JWST consensus models predicted. Leading explanations: bursty star formation, top-heavy stellar populations, or less dust. None of these requires breaking ΛCDM yet. Next Data to Watch # DESI final-year analyses. Euclid DR1 (first major cosmology release, scheduled late Oct 2026, ~2,000 deg²): watch for weak-lensing constraints on dark energy and gravity. The March 2025 quick release already showed ~500 strong-lens candidates and a 380,000-galaxy morphology catalogue. Rubin LSST supernova and weak-lensing samples (survey started 2026-06-30). New JWST record attempts at z > 15. Sources # DESI DR2 results, Ohio State News (2025-03-19): https://news.osu.edu/new-desi-results-strengthen-hints-that-dark-energy-may-evolve UT Dallas, “Evidence mounts for evolving dark energy” (2025-03-19): https://news.utdallas.edu/science-technology/desi-results-dark-energy-2025 IFAE, DESI DR2 BAO summary: https://cosmolya.ifae.es/post/2025-desi-dr2-bao/ Live Science, MoM-z14: https://www.livescience.com/space/astronomy/previously-unimaginable-james-webb-telescope-breaks-own-record-again-discovering-farthest-known-galaxy-in-the-universe Naidu et al., “A Cosmic Miracle” (OJAp 2026): https://doi.org/10.33232/001c.156033 Physics World, CCHP 70.39 and reactions: https://physicsworld.com/a/cosmic-conflict-continues-new-data-fuel-the-hubble-tension-debate/ Live Science, Freedman vs Riess: https://www.livescience.com/space/cosmology/one-of-the-universe-s-biggest-paradoxes-could-be-even-weirder-than-we-thought-james-webb-telescope-study-reveals Euclid DR1 schedule (EAS 2026 symposium): https://eas.unige.ch/EAS_meeting/session.jsp?id=S10 Paper analyses: ../papers/desi-2025-dr2-dark-energy.md , ../papers/naidu-2026-mom-z14.md , ../papers/freedman-2025-cchp-h0.md Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble%27s_law#Hubble_tension

t: Research Now: Gravitational Waves and Black Holes
d: GW250114, the area law, catalogue growth and what LVK's O4/O5 runs will deliver.
x: Status date: November 15, 2026. Concepts # Gravitational waves: ripples in spacetime from accelerating masses. LIGO’s 4 km arms change length by less than a proton’s width as a wave passes. Three phases of a merger signal: 1. Inspiral: a “chirp” as frequency and amplitude rise. 2. Merger. 3. Ringdown: the new black hole settles, emitting quasi-normal modes (“tones”). Kerr metric: a spinning black hole is described completely by mass and spin. Its ringdown frequencies are fixed by those two numbers, which makes the ringdown a direct test. Hawking area theorem (1971): in classical general relativity, total event-horizon area never decreases. Bekenstein and Hawking tied that area to entropy , so this is the black-hole second law of thermodynamics. GW250114 (LVK, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 111403, Sept 2025) # Signal-to-noise ratio ≈ 80 in the two LIGO detectors. Near-equal masses: 33.6 and 32.2 M☉ , small spins (χ ≤ 0.26), negligible eccentricity. Area law: Pre-merger total ≈ 240,000 km². My check from the published masses gives ≈237,000 km² for non-spinning horizons (see the figure). Remnant ≈ 400,000 km². Result consistent with the area law at ~99.999% credibility. The 2021 test with GW150914 reached ~95%. Kerr test: the dominant (ℓ=|m|=2) mode and its first overtone were identified, with frequencies matching Kerr predictions to within ±30%. Why it matters # It is the cleanest empirical check yet of black-hole thermodynamics, where gravity meets quantum physics. Louder signals mean better tests of general relativity. Next-generation detectors (Cosmic Explorer, Einstein Telescope, LISA) will push this to “spectroscopy” of many modes. Open Questions # How do black holes in the “pair-instability gap” (~60–130 M☉) form? Hierarchical mergers are one possibility. Is there any deviation from Kerr at higher overtone precision? d: Up-to-date status of Mercury to Pluto, from BepiColombo to Mars sample-return news.
x: Status date: November 15, 2026. Mars # Context Jezero Crater held a lake more than 3.5 billion years ago. Perseverance has been exploring it since February 2021. Sapphire Canyon (sample 25) Drilled in July 2024 from the rock “Cheyava Falls” in the Bright Angel formation on the edge of Neretva Vallis. Shows “leopard spots”: concentric reaction fronts where redox-sensitive minerals sit next to organic matter. Published in Nature on 2025-09-10 (“Redox-driven mineral and organic associations in Jezero Crater, Mars”) and described by NASA as a potential biosignature , not a detection of life. The decisive tests need the core back on Earth, and the Mars Sample Return architecture is being restructured. Open question : can non-biological low-temperature chemistry make the same textures? (See the ../astrobiology/ track.) Europa (Jupiter) # An ice shell over a global salty ocean, kept liquid by tidal heating. Europa Clipper : launched 2024-10-14, Mars gravity assist on 2025-03-01, Earth gravity assist on 2026-12-03 , arrives at Jupiter in April 2030 for 49 planned Europa flybys. It is a Jupiter orbiter, not a lander. ESA’s JUICE is also on its way to Jupiter, which allows coordinated science. Enceladus (Saturn) # Its south-polar plumes spray ocean water into space, and Cassini sampled them directly. Organics, salts and phosphates have been detected in that material. This is the most accessible ocean in the Solar System. Titan (Saturn) # Thick nitrogen atmosphere, methane rain, hydrocarbon lakes, and a water ocean under the crust. NASA’s Dragonfly rotorcraft is in development to study prebiotic chemistry on the surface. Kamoʻoalewa (near-Earth quasi-moon) # Asteroid 469219 Kamoʻoalewa (2016 HO3) co-orbits the Sun with Earth. Tianwen-2 (CNSA) launched in May 2025 and arrived in July 2026 , imaging the body from about 20 km. Early reports put its diameter at ~18 m and its spectrum closer to an ordinary silicate asteroid. That weakens the leading “lunar fragment” origin idea, but the samples will decide. Plan: leave in April 2027, sample capsule returns in late November 2027, then continue on to main-belt comet 311P/PANSTARRS. d: Current results on stellar evolution and exoplanet atmospheres from JWST, TESS and Gaia.
x: Status date: November 15, 2026. Concepts # Hydrostatic balance A star is a fight between gravity pulling in and gas plus radiation pressure pushing out. Fusion in the core supplies the pressure. Mass–luminosity relation On the main sequence, L ∝ M^~3.5. Doubling a star’s mass makes it ~11× brighter. Lifetime scaling Fuel ∝ M and burn rate ∝ L, so lifetime t ≈ 10 Gyr × (M/M☉)^-2.5. Sun ≈ 10 Gyr, a 10 M☉ star ≈ 30 Myr, a 0.5 M☉ red dwarf ≈ 57 Gyr (longer than the universe has existed). End states by initial mass (working) < ~8 M☉: red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf (the Sun’s fate). ~8–20 M☉: core-collapse supernova → neutron star. ~20 M☉: supernova or direct collapse → black hole. Hertzsprung–Russell diagram Plots luminosity against surface temperature. Main-sequence stars lie on a diagonal band; giants sit above it and white dwarfs below it (see png/hr_diagram_generated.png ). Exoplanet Core # Detection methods Transit: the dip in starlight as a planet crosses its star. More than two-thirds of confirmed planets. Radial velocity: the star wobbles towards and away from us. Microlensing, direct imaging and timing make up the rest. Count The NASA Exoplanet Archive passed 6,000 confirmed planets in September 2025 (6,007 at the time of the announcement), with more than 8,000 candidates awaiting confirmation. It had reached 5,000 in March 2022. Why red dwarfs dominate rocky-planet studies Small star + small planet = deep transit; close-in habitable zones = frequent transits. Examples: TRAPPIST-1e and Proxima b (see ../planetary/png/habitable_zones_generated.png ). Downside: flares and strong winds may strip the atmospheres of planets that close to the star. Open Questions # Can rocky planets around active M dwarfs keep their atmospheres? JWST thermal-emission results on TRAPPIST-1 b and c so far point to thin or absent atmospheres. What sets the “radius valley” between super-Earths and sub-Neptunes: photoevaporation or core-powered mass loss? How common are true Earth analogues (Earth-size, 1 AU orbit, Sun-like star)? Current surveys are biased against finding them. Dated Studies # 2025-09: NASA Exoplanet Archive reaches 6,000 confirmed exoplanets. 2026-06-30: Vera C. Rubin Observatory starts its 10-year LSST, which will catch huge numbers of variable stars, supernovae and transients (see ../exploration/missions-and-instruments.md ). d: Sapphire Canyon, K2-18 b, TRAPPIST-1e and the standards of evidence for life.
x: Status date: November 15, 2026. Concepts # Habitability ≠ inhabited The working requirements are liquid water, an energy source and the elements CHNOPS. Places that have all three are candidates, not detections. Biosignature A substance, pattern or structure that life could produce. It only becomes evidence after non-biological routes have been ruled out in that specific environment . CoLD scale (Green et al., Nature 2021) 1. Detect a possible signal 2. Rule out contamination / instrument artefacts 3. Show biology could produce it in that environment 4. Rule out non-biological sources 5. Find an additional, independent signal 6. Rule out alternative hypotheses 7. Confirm predictions with follow-up observations The placements in png/cold_scale_generated.png are my own working reading of the literature, not an official ranking. Case Studies # K2-18 b — DMS/DMDS in a sub-Neptune atmosphere # 2023 and April 2025 (Madhusudhan et al.): JWST spectra interpreted as showing dimethyl sulfide and/or dimethyl disulfide. On Earth, DMS comes from marine microbes. The authors proposed a “Hycean” ocean world. Pushback: A NASA-led joint reanalysis (preprint, July 2025) found no conclusive DMS and showed that non-biological chemistry can make DMS in hydrogen-rich atmospheres. The Astronomical Journal , October 2025: the MIRI signal is dominated by instrument systematics (red noise), and most retrievals with their preferred binning do not favour DMS/DMDS. What is robust: methane and CO₂ are detected. Status: contested signal (CoLD 1). Mars — Sapphire Canyon “leopard spots” # Redox-mineral reaction fronts next to organic matter in 3.5-billion-year-old lake mudstone ( Nature , 2025-09-10). Called a potential biosignature. The key remaining step is ruling out low-temperature non-biological reactions, which really needs Earth labs. Status: strongest Mars candidate so far, CoLD 1 (moving toward 2–3 if samples return). Venus — phosphine (2020) # A reported phosphine line in the cloud deck. Later reanalyses questioned the calibration and suggested sulfur dioxide or non-biological explanations. Status: disputed. TRAPPIST-1 e — does a habitable-zone Earth-size planet have air? # JWST NIRSpec/PRISM, 4 transits analysed (DREAMS collaboration; Espinoza et al. and Glidden et al., ApJL 990, Sept 2025). Results: A primordial hydrogen atmosphere is ruled out, and a CO₂-dominated (Venus/Mars-like) atmosphere is unlikely. The best fit is an N₂-rich atmosphere with trace CH₄ , but a bare rock still cannot be rejected. Starspots on the host star contaminate the spectra. A new program pairs back-to-back transits of TRAPPIST-1 e and the airless TRAPPIST-1 b to subtract the star’s signal. ~15 more transits are planned. Status: habitability test in progress; no biosignature claim. Enceladus — plume chemistry # Organics, salts and phosphates in ocean spray show the ocean is habitable (energy + chemistry). That is not a life signal in itself. Status: strong habitability evidence; no biosignature claim. Lessons (my working notes) # Extraordinary claims need independent instruments , not just re-binning the same data. Context matters. The same molecule can be biological on Earth and non-biological on a hydrogen-rich world. Missions should be designed for steps 2–4 of CoLD, not just step 1. Mars sample return and the Habitable Worlds Observatory are aimed at this. d: Analysis of DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations and the 2.8–4.2σ evolving dark energy hint.

Citation: DESI Collaboration, DESI DR2 Results II: Measurements of Baryon Acoustic Oscillations and Cosmological Constraints (arXiv:2503.14738, released 19 March 2025) Access: 🔓 arXiv Analysis basis: abstract, collaboration and university releases (OSU, UT Dallas, IFAE, Ohio U.) and coverage. Full text not read here. Question # Does the expansion history traced by baryon acoustic oscillations still fit a cosmological constant, or does dark energy change over time? Method # Three years of spectroscopic data: ~15 million galaxies and quasars, including Lyman-α forest BAO at high z. The dataset is more than twice the size of DR1. Blinded analysis , so the results stay hidden from the team until the pipeline is frozen. Fits ΛCDM and the w0–wa (CPL) dark-energy model, alone and combined with CMB (Planck/ACT) and supernovae (Pantheon+, Union3, DESY5). Key Results # DESI alone is consistent with ΛCDM. DESI + CMB + supernovae prefer evolving dark energy at 2.8–4.2σ , depending on the supernova sample. This is stronger than DR1. The preferred region has w0 > −1 and wa < 0. Dark energy would have been stronger in the recent past and is weakening today. There is a possible “phantom crossing” (w < −1) at earlier times; see ../cosmology/png/dark_energy_evolution_generated.png . DR1 public data released alongside. Strengths # Largest 3D map yet; blinding; multiple independent tracers. Several different external datasets point the same way. Limitations and Critiques # Not 5σ. Significance depends heavily on which supernova compilation is used, which suggests supernova calibration systematics could drive part of the signal. The w0–wa form is a convenient fit, not a physical model. Different parameterisations can shift the conclusion. Internal team members themselves call it “too early to claim categorically”. Links # ../cosmology/cosmology-core.md (Live Debate 1) My Take # This is the most important open question in cosmology right now. The fact that DESI alone agrees with Λ, while the tension appears only in combinations, makes cross-dataset systematics the first suspect. Euclid DR1 (late 2026) and the DESI final data are the independent checks. Follow-ups # Repeat with recalibrated supernova samples, and with Euclid weak lensing. Test physically motivated models (quintessence, interacting dark energy) instead of CPL.

d: The loudest black-hole merger yet and a test of black-hole thermodynamics.
x: How to read this analysis Each analysis follows the same template: citation, access, question, method, results, strengths, limitations, links, assessment and follow-ups. Use Open PDF to read it in a new tab or Download PDF to save it. Citation: LVK Collaboration, Physical Review Letters 135(11), 111403 (Sept 2025) Access: 🔓 CC-BY 4.0 (open) Analysis basis: published abstract, LIGO science summary and coverage. Question # Can one very loud merger directly test that (1) total horizon area never decreases and (2) the remnant is a Kerr black hole? Method # Signal detected on 14 Jan 2025 by both LIGO detectors at a network SNR of ~80. Separate analyses of inspiral (initial areas) and post-merger ringdown (final area). Some analyses exclude up to five of the strongest merger cycles to avoid modelling bias. The ringdown is fitted with Kerr quasi-normal modes. Key Results # Masses 33.6 (+1.2/−0.8) and 32.2 (+0.8/−1.3) M☉; spins ≤ 0.26; eccentricity ≤ 0.03. Final area greater than total initial area at high credibility (~99.999%), versus ~95% from GW150914 in 2021. Areas go from ≈240,000 km² before to ≈400,000 km² after. The fundamental ℓ=|m|=2 mode and its first overtone were identified, with frequencies within ±30% of Kerr predictions. Strengths # Very high SNR; tests designed to be robust to merger-phase modelling. Near-twin of GW150914, so it shows how far detector sensitivity has improved (~3× clearer). Limitations and Critiques # ±30% on mode frequencies still leaves room for small deviations from Kerr. The area law is a classical result. Quantum effects (Hawking radiation) are far too small to see here. Links # ../black-holes-gw/ : my independent check of the pre-merger area (~237,000 km² from the published masses) matches the reported ~240,000 km². My Take # This is a textbook-level confirmation that can be reproduced with a calculator. That makes it great teaching material, and it’s in the black-holes figure.

Retrievals across many atmospheric compositions and pressures; modelling of stellar contamination. Key Results # No primordial H₂/He atmosphere , likely stripped by the flaring star. A CO₂-dominated atmosphere (Venus- or Mars-like) is unlikely . Trace CH₄ in an N₂-rich atmosphere fits acceptably , but the data cannot reject a bare rock . Starspots on TRAPPIST-1 imprint features that mimic or mask planetary ones. Strengths # Careful null-hypothesis framing; explicit treatment of the star. Limitations # Only four transits. Different visits disagree (July vs October 2023), so stellar variability matters. What’s next # About 15 more transits, including back-to-back transits with TRAPPIST-1 b (airless) to subtract the star’s contribution. Roughly 20 transits are expected in total. Links # ../astrobiology/ · ../planetary/png/habitable_zones_generated.png · lab: ../labs/transit-lab.html My Take # This is the best near-term test of whether rocky planets around M dwarfs can stay habitable. The b/e differencing trick is clever, and the result will shape the target list for the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

d: The smallest planet and closest to the Sun, a cratered iron-rich world with almost no atmosphere.
x: Surface # Heavily cratered like the Moon, with huge cliffs (lobate scarps) formed as the planet cooled and shrank; ice hides in permanently shadowed polar craters. Atmosphere # An ultra-thin exosphere of sodium, potassium and oxygen blasted off the surface by solar wind. Interior # An enormous iron core makes up ~85% of its radius; it has a weak global magnetic field. Exploration # Mariner 10 (1974–75), MESSENGER (orbited 2011–15) and BepiColombo (ESA–JAXA), which entered orbit around Mercury on 21 November 2026. Quick facts # Biggest day–night temperature swing of any planet Its year is shorter than two of its solar days Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet)

d: Earth's 'twin' in size, with a runaway greenhouse that makes it the hottest planet.
x: Surface # Volcanic plains, pancake domes and highland ‘continents’ (Ishtar, Aphrodite); possibly active volcanoes today (Maat Mons changes seen in Magellan data). Atmosphere # Crushing CO₂ atmosphere 92 times Earth’s surface pressure, with sulfuric-acid clouds and winds that circle the planet in 4 days (super-rotation). Interior # Rocky with an iron core, but no measurable magnetic field. Exploration # Venera landers (USSR) returned the first images from another planet’s surface (1975); Magellan radar-mapped it; future missions DAVINCI, VERITAS and EnVision. Quick facts # Spins backwards A day is longer than its year Phosphine detection (2020) is disputed Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus

d: The only known world with life, liquid surface oceans and active plate tectonics.
x: Surface # 71% ocean; plate tectonics recycles the crust and regulates climate over millions of years. Atmosphere # 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen; ozone layer shields UV; strong magnetic field deflects solar wind. Interior # Iron-nickel core generates the geodynamo; mantle convection drives plates. Exploration # Observed by thousands of satellites; humans have lived continuously in orbit since 2000 (ISS). Quick facts # Densest planet Only planet not named after a god Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth

d: A cold desert world with the largest volcano and canyon in the solar system and a watery past.
x: Surface # Olympus Mons (~22 km high), Valles Marineris (~4,000 km long), ancient river deltas such as Jezero, polar ice caps of water and CO₂. Atmosphere # Thin CO₂ atmosphere (<1% of Earth’s pressure); global dust storms. Interior # Lost its global magnetic field ~4 billion years ago; InSight measured a liquid iron core and marsquakes. Exploration # Viking (1976), Spirit and Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance with Ingenuity helicopter, China’s Zhurong, India’s Mangalyaan (2014, first Asian Mars orbiter, first-attempt success). Quick facts # Perseverance found a ‘potential biosignature’ at Sapphire Canyon (2025) Mars Sample Return was cancelled in 2026 Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars

d: The giant of the solar system, more than twice as massive as all other planets combined.
x: Surface # No solid surface; colourful belts and zones; the Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has raged for at least 190 years. Atmosphere # Hydrogen and helium with ammonia clouds; lightning and auroras. Interior # Metallic hydrogen layer creates the strongest planetary magnetic field; Juno found a ‘fuzzy’, dilute core. Exploration # Pioneer, Voyager, Galileo (1995–2003), Juno (since 2016), ESA’s JUICE (arrives 2031), Europa Clipper (arrives 2030). Quick facts # Shortest day of any planet Its magnetosphere is the largest structure in the solar system Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter

d: The ringed planet, so low in density it would float in a big enough bathtub.
x: Surface # Gaseous; a hexagonal jet stream at its north pole. Atmosphere # Hydrogen and helium; winds up to 1,800 km/h. Interior # Rocky-icy core within metallic hydrogen; rings made of mostly water ice, possibly only a few hundred million years old. Exploration # Pioneer 11, Voyagers, Cassini–Huygens (2004–2017, ended by diving into Saturn); Dragonfly to Titan launches ~2028. Quick facts # Has the most known moons Rings are ~280,000 km wide but often only ~10 m thick Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn

d: An ice giant tipped on its side, rolling around the Sun with extreme seasons.
x: Surface # Blue-green from methane; faint rings. Atmosphere # Hydrogen, helium, methane; coldest planetary atmosphere measured (−224°C). Interior # Water, ammonia and methane ‘ices’ around a rocky core; offset, tilted magnetic field. Exploration # Only Voyager 2 (1986) has visited; a Uranus Orbiter and Probe is the top US flagship priority. Quick facts # Axial tilt ~98° Each pole gets 42 years of sunlight then 42 of darkness Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus

d: The most distant planet, found by mathematics before it was seen.

d: The best-known dwarf planet, with nitrogen glaciers and a heart-shaped plain.

Interior # Rocky core with an icy mantle. Exploration # Discovered by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930; reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006; New Horizons flew by in 2015. x: How it works # Gravity squeezes the core to ~15 million K, where hydrogen fuses; outward radiation pressure balances gravity in hydrostatic equilibrium. Evidence # The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram; helioseismology of the Sun. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_sequence

d: The most common stars in the galaxy (~75%), small, cool and able to shine for trillions of years.
x: How it works # Low mass (0.08–0.6 Sun) means slow fusion and fully convective interiors that mix fuel. Evidence # Proxima Centauri, TRAPPIST-1; frequent flares challenge habitability of their planets. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_dwarf

d: 'Failed stars' between ~13 and ~80 Jupiter masses that never sustain hydrogen fusion.
x: How it works # Too light to fuse ordinary hydrogen; they briefly burn deuterium and then cool for ever. Evidence # First confirmed in 1995 (Gliese 229B, Teide 1); WISE found the coldest, near room temperature. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_dwarf

d: What Sun-like stars become when core hydrogen runs out: swollen to hundreds of times their size.
x: How it works # The core contracts and heats while a hydrogen-burning shell inflates the outer layers; later helium ignites in a ‘helium flash’. Evidence # Arcturus, Aldebaran; the Sun will become one in ~5 billion years. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_giant

d: The largest and most luminous stars, destined to explode.
x: How it works # Massive stars (>8 Suns) fuse heavier elements in shells like an onion up to iron. Evidence # Betelgeuse, Rigel, UY Scuti, Eta Carinae. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergiant_star

d: The hot, Earth-sized remnant core of a Sun-like star, supported by electron degeneracy pressure.
x: How it works # After a red giant sheds a planetary nebula, the exposed core (mostly carbon and oxygen) slowly cools; maximum mass ~1.4 Suns (Chandrasekhar limit). Evidence # Sirius B; ~97% of all stars will end this way. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_dwarf

d: A white dwarf cooled until it no longer glows, which takes far longer than the universe's current age.
x: How it works # Cooling over ~10¹⁵ years. Evidence # None exist yet: the universe is only 13.8 billion years old. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_dwarf

d: The collapsed core of a massive star: more mass than the Sun packed into a city-sized ball ~20 km across.
x: How it works # In a core-collapse supernova, electrons and protons merge into neutrons; neutron degeneracy halts the collapse. Evidence # A teaspoon weighs ~a billion tonnes; NICER measures their sizes. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_star

d: A spinning neutron star sweeping radio beams across Earth like a lighthouse.
x: How it works # Strong magnetic fields channel radiation from the poles; rotation makes it pulse. Evidence # Discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell in 1967; millisecond pulsars spin over 700 times a second. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulsar

d: Neutron stars with the strongest magnetic fields in the universe (~10¹⁵ gauss).
x: How it works # Decaying magnetic fields crack the crust, releasing giant flares; linked to some fast radio bursts. Evidence # SGR 1806-20’s 2004 giant flare; SGR 1935+2154 produced a fast radio burst in 2020. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetar

d: Pulsating stars whose period reveals their true brightness, used as cosmic distance markers.
x: How it works # Layers of ionised helium trap and release heat, driving pulsations. Evidence # Henrietta Leavitt’s 1912 period–luminosity law let Hubble measure distances to galaxies. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cepheid_variable

d: Hot, massive stars stripping off their own outer layers in violent winds.
x: How it works # Intense radiation drives winds that expose helium-, carbon- or nitrogen-rich layers. Evidence # WR 104, WR 140 dust shells imaged by JWST. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf%25E2%2580%2593Rayet_star

d: The explosion of a massive star whose iron core collapses in under a second.
x: How it works # Iron cannot release energy by fusion; the core collapses into a neutron star or black hole and the rebound plus neutrinos blow the star apart. Evidence # SN 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud, the first detected by neutrinos; it forged and scattered elements like oxygen and calcium. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernova

d: A white dwarf exploding after gaining too much mass, a 'standard candle' that revealed dark energy.
x: How it works # Accretion from a companion or a white-dwarf merger triggers runaway carbon fusion. Evidence # 1998 discovery of the accelerating universe (Nobel Prize 2011). Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_Ia_supernova

d: The explosion when two neutron stars merge, forging gold, platinum and other heavy elements.
x: How it works # Rapid neutron capture (r-process) in ejected neutron-rich matter. Evidence # GW170817 (2017): gravitational waves plus light from the same event, first multi-messenger observation. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilonova

x: How it works # Long bursts come from collapsing massive stars (collapsars); short bursts from neutron star mergers. Evidence # GRB 221009A (2022), the ‘BOAT’, brightest of all time. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma-ray_burst

d: A white dwarf flaring as hydrogen from a companion ignites on its surface.
x: How it works # Thermonuclear runaway on the surface; the star survives and can repeat. Evidence # T Coronae Borealis, a recurrent nova, was expected to erupt in 2024–26. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova

x: How it works # In globular cluster cores, close encounters merge stars into ‘blue stragglers’. Evidence # V1309 Scorpii (2008) was seen merging as a ‘red nova’. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_collision

d: Galaxies merge over hundreds of millions of years; stars rarely touch but gas collapses into new stars.
